extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, computer scientists, and technical authors (students and authors preparing papers, books, algorithms, or literate programs)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for clear mathematical exposition, typesetting, presentation of formulas/algorithms, and literate programming — aimed at authors preparing papers, books, exercises, and program documentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid psychologically bad line breaks
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not let a final symbol lie on a line separate from the rest of its sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use non-breaking spaces (e.g., a tilde '~' in TeX) or processor-specific methods to tie tokens together so that awkward breaks are prevented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use spell-checkers
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors who are not strong spellers should learn to use spelling checkers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many people differ in spelling ability; automated spelling tools catch common errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep formulas reasonably short and modular ('name and conquer')
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid allowing formulas to get so long that they do not format well or become unnecessarily confusing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce names or group subexpressions so that frequently manipulated pieces remain as units; restructure math to maintain manageable formula units.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be stingy with quotation marks
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid overusing quotation marks (e.g., 'three cute things in quotes' is too cute).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotation marks should be used sparingly to avoid affectation or confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize unnecessary subscripts
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't overuse subscripts which make expressions hard to read.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose clearer notations or renumber/rename variables so that highly subscripted expressions are simplified and less ambiguous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize theorem/lemma in titles
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize words like 'Theorem' and 'Lemma' when used in titles (e.g., Lemma 1, Theorem 23).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistent capitalization signals formal statements and improves clarity in headings and references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place words between adjacent formulas for clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid leaving formulas adjacent without intervening words when the resulting sentence is ambiguous (e.g., 'Add k times to c.').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Insert short phrases so the sentence clearly expresses the intended operation (e.g., 'Add k times to c' -> 'Add k copies of ... to c' or rephrase).

rubrics_metrics.name: Define symbols before (or very near) use
rubrics_metrics.description: Be careful to define symbols before you use them or at least very near where they are first used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers should not be forced to hunt for definitions; local placement improves comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid monotonous sentence openings; use parallelism appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't get hung up on one or two sentence styles (e.g., repeatedly starting sentences with 'Thus', 'Consequently', 'Therefore').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vary sentence openings for readability; keep parallelism when it is rhetorically or logically appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write sentences comprehensible left-to-right
rubrics_metrics.description: Structure sentences so readers can follow the intended meaning as they read left to right; avoid constructions that suggest you're proving the conditions themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For example, prefer 'We prove that the two conditions (grunt) and (snort) imply (blah)' over 'We prove that (grunt) and (snort) implies (blah)'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'that' according to cadence and clarity — read aloud
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidelines for using the word 'that' depend on cadence and clarity of the sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide placement of 'that' by reading sentences aloud to judge clarity and rhythm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of tone/formality of words like 'shall'
rubrics_metrics.description: The word 'shall' reads as formal to younger audiences and may be natural in definitions for some readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select register appropriate to the target audience; avoid stilted formality unless required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be precise in logical wording
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid imprecise formulations (e.g., 'not nonincreasing' vs 'increasing') that can change meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write the precise logical condition intended; illustrate distinction with examples (P_{j+1} for some j vs all j).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid passive voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer active constructions to passive ones (e.g., replace 'It can be shown...' with 'A proof shows...').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Active voice is clearer and more direct; reduces vagueness about the agent of action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mixed tenses on the same subject
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep tense usage consistent for a given subject to avoid awkwardness (e.g., mixing 'assume now' with 'will show').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose appropriate tense (present for timeless facts, past when discussing what was done) and apply consistently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phrase proofs by contradiction clearly
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid clumsy phrases like 'Assume by contradiction that (blah)'; instead say 'The proof that (blah) is by contradiction' or 'To prove (grunt), let us assume the opposite...'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use natural explanatory phrasing that makes the method clear and readable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use conversational tone with signposts and transitions
rubrics_metrics.description: A conversational tone with signposts and clear transition paragraphs makes proofs pleasant to read.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short informal remarks (e.g., 'The lemma is half proved') and explicit division of proof parts help the reader follow arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose relation notation consistent with prior context
rubrics_metrics.description: Either use symbolic tuple/list notation or inequality notation in a way consistent with earlier exposition to aid visualization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you wrote 'P = (P1, P2, ... , Pn)' earlier, use the form the reader expects; keep ordering and relative positions consistent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use professional designers and copy editors when preparing books
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors preparing books should not forget the value of professional book designers and copy editors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designers determine page templates, fonts, headings, and other typographic details; copy editors catch punctuation and stylistic errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rewrite in multiple passes and formats
rubrics_metrics.description: Rewriting should occur across stages: handwritten drafts, typing and editing for flow, TeXing, and further passes; different passes reveal different issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many successful writers perform several drafts; sometimes starting over after months yields improvements, but eventually you must publish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish mathematical numerals from text numerals when using special fonts
rubrics_metrics.description: When using a math-specific font (e.g., Euler), mathematical numerals may differ from text numerals and must be distinguished carefully.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Book preparation should mark mathematical numerals differently from textual numerals so zeros and digit shapes are appropriate to context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose phrasing by ear for small style choices ('all' vs 'all of', position of 'only', 'also')
rubrics_metrics.description: Small stylistic choices should be decided by listening to phrasing; shift words during editing for best flow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use your ear when editing; try various positions of adverbs/particles to improve cadence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give motivation before stating a rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Tell readers why something is true or valuable before stressing the rule itself to avoid leaving readers wondering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Split into paragraphs if needed: motivate first, then state the identity/rule and its significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid awkward repeated prepositions ('replace by'/'replace with')
rubrics_metrics.description: Phrases like 'by replacing ... by ...' are bad; prefer rephrasing (e.g., 'by changing ... to ...').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose alternate constructions to avoid repetition and awkwardness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read at speed to judge rhythm
rubrics_metrics.description: Reading your text at normal speed helps sense sentence rhythm and catch awkward constructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this method during editing to improve flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not display false equations as if true
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid typesetting false equations as normal displayed math; if using them as examples, mark them explicitly (e.g., 'the equation ... is always false!').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers' eyes may treat displayed equations as authoritative; mark counterexamples or false formulas clearly in text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure clear pronoun antecedents
rubrics_metrics.description: Be sure the antecedent of any pronoun is clear; ambiguous uses of 'it' or similar can confuse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rewrite sentences so 'it' or 'this' unambiguously refers to a previously mentioned object or idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid page breaks in middle of displayed formulas
rubrics_metrics.description: Near the end of editing, ensure displayed formulas are not split across pages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Add or change text to fill or clear pages so displayed formulas appear entirely on one page; treat pagination as part of final editing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order proofs in the same order as definitions/cases
rubrics_metrics.description: When dealing with several separate cases, let proofs follow the same order as earlier definitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistency of order helps reader orientation and comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use correct dashes: hyphen, en-dash, minus sign, em-dash
rubrics_metrics.description: Hyphens, en-dashes, minus signs, and em-dashes are distinct and should not be used interchangeably.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hyphen: shortest (compound words); en-dash: ranges (e.g., lines 10–18); minus sign: used in formulas; em-dash: sentence-level interruption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofread for mathematics as well as prose
rubrics_metrics.description: When proofreading, check technical correctness and not just stylistic issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: clarify limit statements ('when x decreases to 0' vs 'x → 0' through negative values) to avoid mathematical errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'instead' with explicit contrast
rubrics_metrics.description: When using 'instead', make the contrast clear in the sentence so the reader immediately understands the reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.g., 'And when x = −1 instead of +1, ...' rather than 'And when x = −1 instead, ...'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use present tense for timeless facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Use present tense for facts that remain true even if proved in the past.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve past tense for events or facts that were found to be false or when narrating historical actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid needless repetition of words within a sentence
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduce repeating the same words in short proximity to improve clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substitute synonyms or rephrase (example shown converting 'fill in the values' to 'fill in the entries').

rubrics_metrics.name: Use page numbers only for remote references
rubrics_metrics.description: Give page numbers only when references are remote; usually citing 'Equation 5.14' or similar suffices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Too many page numbers become unwieldy; adopt economical referencing practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select formula presentation form to fit horizontal/vertical space; be consistent
rubrics_metrics.description: Choosing inline limits vs. above-and-below limits trades horizontal for vertical space; pick a form that fits and strive for consistency throughout a book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both forms are used in practice; the choice depends on page width and personal/book style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Break long formulas logically; consider changing math to improve layout
rubrics_metrics.description: When long formulas don't fit, break lines at logical places or introduce new symbols; sometimes move expressions to displayed form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In inline formulas break after '='; in displayed formulas break before '='; authors may change math presentation to ease placement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Edit sentences/paragraphs for flow but preserve clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Change semicolons to periods or vice versa, and break paragraphs where necessary, but ensure resulting constructions are unambiguous (especially sentences starting with conjunctions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use smaller paragraphs to improve readability; verify antecedents of pronouns remain clear after edits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose clear and non-misleading variable names
rubrics_metrics.description: Variable names that are too similar for conceptually unrelated variables are confusing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systematic renaming using a text editor is useful to disambiguate and improve readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overuse of stacked fractions; prefer slash form when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Stacked fractions with horizontal bars can produce tiny numerals (especially in exponents); copy editors often slash fractions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When slashing, add parentheses where necessary to preserve meaning; use form that improves legibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make exercises unambiguous with carefully chosen redundancy
rubrics_metrics.description: Since exercises have little context, ambiguity is particularly harmful; include redundancy as needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carefully state assumptions and desired results in exercises; this also aids translation to other languages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credit sources for exercises and traced results
rubrics_metrics.description: Due to copyright law changes, give credit to previously published exercises and historical sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citing sources is usually sufficient; tracing the original source of some theorems may be difficult but try to credit appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short, pithy answers (even starting with a symbol) are acceptable for exercise solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: When writing answers to exercises, terse and symbol-starting answers are sometimes appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rhetorical guidelines may be relaxed in exercise answers where brevity is useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present algorithms in English and with labeled steps
rubrics_metrics.description: To avoid alienating readers by choosing a specific programming language, present algorithms in English with numbered/labeled steps, comments, and high-level flowcharts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Knuth's style treats algorithms like theorems: numbered steps with parenthetical remarks (often invariants) and occasional flowcharts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt a personal, consistent style for algorithm presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal styles are acceptable but must be used consistently; copying someone else's style without understanding conventions leads to poor results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a style that works for you and apply it throughout a project; Knuth used pidgin Algol in later work but kept early series consistent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat programs as literature — write for humans and for correctness
rubrics_metrics.description: A computer program should be crafted like literature: clear exposition benefits both readers and program correctness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thinking about program structure and exposition can lead to better running code and easier verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain complex things twice (informally and formally) and break into parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Present a concept/module informally to motivate it, then give the formal version; break large systems into manageable modules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle underlies WEB and literate programming: modules begin with text and end with formal code; explain both intuitively and rigorously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use tools like WEB to produce both typeset documentation and source code from one file
rubrics_metrics.description: Systems like WEB let a single source file generate a typesetting file or a programming-language source file depending on the processing tool used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This supports literate programming workflows where documentation and code are co-developed and synchronized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Name modules using imperatives for actions and descriptors for declarative modules; capitalize first letter
rubrics_metrics.description: Module names that perform actions should be imperatives (e.g., 'Store the word in the dictionary'), while declarative modules should be descriptors (e.g., 'Procedures for sorting'); capitalize the first letter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear module names communicate intent; follow the module-naming convention appropriate to the module's function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include informal but clear high-level descriptions in each module
rubrics_metrics.description: Modules should contain a concise, informal explanation of what they do that conveys intuition rather than a literal play-by-play.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid step-by-step narration; provide a high-level account that helps readers understand design and intention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep modules small and manageable (around a dozen lines)
rubrics_metrics.description: Modules that are too long should be split into smaller pieces to reflect the philosophy of breaking complex things into tractable parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When modules grow unwieldy, cut them into multiple modules with clear boundaries to improve readability and maintainability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid carrying obsolete conventions into new styles
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not carry excess baggage from older styles (e.g., comments after each 'end' used in Pascal) into newer systems like WEB if they are unnecessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When adopting a new style or system, shed outdated conventions and adopt the idioms appropriate to the new environment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose and keep consistent a narrative voice for program descriptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether to describe program actions in first-person plural ('we') or in third-person ('it') and be consistent; Knuth favors 'we'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistency helps readers conceptualize program behavior; be aware of differing opinions (e.g., Dijkstra's objections to anthropomorphizing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't start sentences with a symbol
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid beginning sentences with a symbol (e.g., 'data assumes that ...'); rewrite to start with words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sentences beginning with symbols are harder to parse and can be rewritten into clearer English-first constructions.
